passage:
Tuesday night.

Today a caller who gave the name Nikita, from my bank's security team, was so friendly. Said my card would be blocked in ten minutes unless I read out the code that had just arrived. I actually had the message open. My thumb was over the digits when I remembered that a bank should never ask for that code.

I said, "Please hold, I'll call the number on the back of my card." The caller's voice went sharp, and then the line went dead. My heart is still racing. I feel silly at how close I came to trusting that warm voice.

Told Amma and my roommate. Amma says anybody can be fooled. I've saved the bank's official number in my phone.

Gautam

qa.q: What name did the caller give?
qa.a: The caller gave the name Nikita, from the bank's security team.

qa.q: Why did Gautam nearly read out the code?
qa.a: The caller was friendly and urgent, saying the card would be blocked in ten minutes, and that mix of warmth and fear almost worked; Gautam even had the message open.

qa.q: What should Gautam do next time a caller says they are from the bank?
qa.a: Never share the code, hang up, and call the official number on the back of the card.

qa.q: How might the caller see Gautam's request to call back?
qa.a: The caller loses the pressure that the trick depends on, which may explain the sharp voice and the sudden hang-up.

grounding: A friendly, urgent caller posing as the bank exploits Gautam's trust and fear; Gautam stops at the last moment and verifies through the official number.
